options.C: To negotiate the final invoice payment
options.D: To delete all data captured during the test from the client's systems
options.E: This is a requirement of the GDPR only

questions.explanation: The debrief bridges technical findings and business understanding. Testers present findings to technical and management stakeholders, explain impact in business terms, and discuss remediation priorities. This ensures the report is actionable and findings are not misinterpreted.

questions.question: A penetration tester accidentally causes a production server to crash during testing. What is the appropriate response?

options.A: Quietly continue testing and mention it in passing in the report appendix
options.B: Immediately notify the client via the emergency contact, document the exact actions that caused the crash, and assist with recovery if possible
options.C: Attempt to restore the server without notifying the client
options.D: Stop all testing and leave the engagement
options.E: Only when performing a white-box test

questions.explanation: Accidental impact on production systems must be immediately disclosed to the client, even if embarrassing. The tester must document precisely what action caused the outage. Good professional conduct and contractual obligations require transparency; attempting to hide the incident would be a serious breach of trust.

questions.question: What is the 'rules of engagement' (RoE) document in the context of a penetration test?

options.A: A legal document that transfers liability from the tester to the client
options.B: A document defining the specific parameters of testing: permitted techniques, testing hours, communication protocols, escalation procedures, and what constitutes success
options.C: A standard contract template from CREST used for all engagements
options.D: A list of CVEs that the tester is authorised to use
options.E: This is handled by the ISP

questions.explanation: Rules of Engagement document the technical and procedural boundaries of the assessment, agreed upon before testing starts. It covers testing windows, permitted techniques (no DoS, social engineering allowed/not), handling of discovered sensitive data, and notification procedures.

questions.question: Why must penetration testers securely delete or return all data obtained from client systems after an engagement?

options.A: To avoid exceeding storage limits on testing machines
options.B: Because contractual, legal, and professional obligations require it; retaining client data (credentials, PII, business data) creates liability and trust issues
options.C: Because the data is encrypted and becomes useless after the engagement key expires
options.D: Only if the data was classified as 'Confidential' or higher
options.E: Only if the tester has a valid security clearance

questions.explanation: Penetration testers routinely access highly sensitive data (credentials, PII, financial records, IP). Contractual obligations (typically in the Statement of Work) and professional ethics require all client data to be securely deleted after the engagement and confirmed in writing.

questions.question: What should a penetration test report's executive summary contain?

options.A: A full technical description of every vulnerability found with proof-of-concept code
options.B: A high-level overview of the engagement, key findings, overall risk rating, and prioritised remediation recommendations — written for non-technical senior management
options.C: A breakdown of the hours spent on each phase of testing
options.D: Raw tool output from Nmap, Nessus, and Burp Suite scans
options.E: This is not a standard part of the penetration testing lifecycle

questions.explanation: The executive summary is written for C-level and board audiences who need to understand business risk without technical detail. It should cover: what was tested, overall security posture, critical issues, and top remediation priorities — all in business language without jargon.

questions.question: What is the primary legal document that authorises a penetration tester to perform testing on a client's systems?

options.B: A signed Statement of Work (SoW) or contract that explicitly authorises the testing activities against the defined scope
options.C: An NDA signed by the tester
options.D: An email from the client's IT manager requesting the test
options.E: Only after the final report has been delivered

questions.explanation: Without explicit written authorisation (SoW, contract, or a specific 'permission to test' letter from the system owner), any penetration testing activity — even well-intentioned — may constitute an offence under the Computer Misuse Act (UK) or equivalent legislation. A signed SoW is essential.

questions.question: During a grey-box penetration test, what information is typically provided to the tester prior to testing?

options.A: No information — the tester must discover everything autonomously
options.B: Full source code, architecture diagrams, and all credentials
options.C: Partial information such as IP ranges, application user credentials, or high-level architecture — simulating a partially informed attacker such as a malicious insider
options.D: Only the name of the target organisation
options.E: This is a requirement of the ISO 27001 standard

questions.explanation: Grey-box testing provides partial knowledge — typically the information a privileged insider or a compromised low-level account would have. This is the most common type of penetration test as it balances realistic threat simulation with testing efficiency.

questions.question: Which Group Policy setting prevents users from accessing the Windows Registry editor (regedit.exe)?

options.A: Restrict access to registry editing tools
options.B: Prevent access to the command prompt
options.C: Do not run specified Windows applications
options.D: Remove Run menu from Start menu
options.E: None of the above

questions.explanation: The 'Prevent access to registry editing tools' Group Policy setting (User Configuration > Administrative Templates > System) disables regedit.exe and regedt32.exe. Attackers may try to circumvent this by using reg.exe from the command line instead.

questions.question: A locked-down Windows desktop has AppLocker enforced but a user finds they can run msbuild.exe to compile and execute C# code. What class of bypass is this?

options.B: A 'living off the land' (LOLBins) AppLocker bypass using a trusted Microsoft-signed binary that can execute arbitrary code
options.C: A kernel driver exploit bypassing AppLocker enforcement
options.D: A UAC bypass used to disable AppLocker
options.E: All of the above

questions.explanation: msbuild.exe is a Microsoft-signed binary (LOLBin) that can build and execute inline C# or VB.NET from a project file. Because it is a trusted signed binary allowed by default AppLocker rules, it bypasses application whitelisting controls.

questions.question: What is the purpose of LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution) in a locked-down desktop environment?

options.A: It removes the local administrator account from all domain-joined machines
options.B: It automatically sets unique, random local administrator passwords per machine, stored in AD and rotated on a schedule, preventing lateral movement via shared local admin credentials
options.C: It enforces a minimum password length of 25 characters for all domain accounts
options.D: It encrypts local administrator credentials using BitLocker
options.E: Only after formal approval from the board of directors

questions.explanation: LAPS solves the problem of all machines sharing the same local admin password — if one is compromised, all are. It randomises each machine's local admin password, stores it in a confidential AD attribute, and rotates it automatically, defeating Pass-the-Hash lateral movement.

questions.question: Which Windows 10/11 feature, when enabled, runs the browser in an isolated Hyper-V container to prevent malware from accessing the host?

options.B: Microsoft Defender Application Guard (MDAG)
options.E: This is not a requirement for CREST certification

questions.explanation: Microsoft Defender Application Guard opens untrusted websites in a hardware-isolated Hyper-V container. Even if a drive-by download fully compromises the browser session, the host system remains protected because the container is destroyed after the session ends.

questions.question: What does 'Controlled Folder Access' in Windows Defender protect against?

options.A: Unauthorised network connections from untrusted applications
options.B: Ransomware and untrusted applications modifying files in protected folders (Documents, Desktop, Pictures) by blocking write access for non-whitelisted processes
options.C: Users accessing system folders without administrative rights
options.D: Outbound data exfiltration from sensitive directories
options.E: It depends on the specific country's jurisdiction

questions.explanation: Controlled Folder Access blocks untrusted processes from modifying files in protected folders. This is a direct anti-ransomware control — even if malware runs on the system, it cannot encrypt files in protected locations unless it is explicitly whitelisted.

questions.question: A penetration tester on a locked-down Windows desktop uses 'certutil -decode base64.txt payload.exe'. What are they exploiting?

options.A: A vulnerability in Windows Certificate Services
options.B: certutil.exe as a LOLBin — a trusted, signed Microsoft binary that can decode base64 and download files, bypassing application whitelisting
options.C: A misconfigured certificate template in Active Directory
options.D: The Windows PKI trust store to sign a malicious executable
options.E: Only when using automated scanning tools

questions.explanation: certutil.exe is a Microsoft-signed binary with multiple dual-use capabilities: base64 encoding/decoding, file downloading (-urlcache -split -f), and hash computation. It is widely abused as a LOLBin to download or decode payloads on systems where direct downloads or unsigned executables are blocked.

questions.question: Which AppLocker rule type provides the strongest and most tamper-resistant control for blocking unsigned executables?

options.A: Path rules based on folder location (e.g., block C:\Users\*)
options.B: Publisher rules based on the software's digital signature (code signing certificate)
options.C: Hash rules based on the SHA-256 hash of the file
options.E: This is handled by the client's internal IT department

questions.explanation: Publisher rules are the most maintainable and tamper-resistant: they allow software from a trusted publisher (e.g., Microsoft) to run even after updates change the binary's hash. Path rules can be bypassed by placing executables in allowed paths; hash rules break on every update.

questions.question: What is the risk of enabling 'Run as Administrator' without UAC prompt for specific applications using a scheduled task with highest privilege?

options.A: The scheduled task consumes excessive CPU resources
options.B: Any user can trigger the scheduled task (if permissions allow), running code as SYSTEM/Administrator without a UAC elevation prompt, providing a UAC bypass path
options.C: The application cannot access network resources when running elevated
options.D: Scheduled tasks with highest privilege automatically expose port 445
options.E: During the post-engagement debrief session

questions.explanation: Creating a scheduled task that runs a writable application with highest privilege is a common UAC bypass and privilege escalation technique. If the task's executable or configuration is writable by standard users, they can hijack it to run arbitrary code as SYSTEM without a UAC prompt.

questions.question: Which Group Policy setting prevents users from installing printer drivers, reducing the risk of PrintNightmare-style attacks on workstations?

options.A: Point and Print Restrictions — require elevated credentials for all printer driver installation
options.B: Disable the Print Spooler service entirely via GPO
options.C: Block inbound TCP 445 via Windows Firewall policy
options.D: Apply WDAC policy blocking driver installation
options.E: Only if the vulnerability is classified as Critical

questions.explanation: The Point and Print Restrictions GPO (Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings) controls which print servers users can install drivers from and whether elevation is required. Properly configuring this prevents unprivileged users from triggering malicious driver installations.

questions.question: Windows Defender Exploit Guard includes Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules. Which ASR rule directly blocks a common macro-based malware delivery technique?

options.A: Block executable content from email client and webmail
options.B: Block Office applications from creating child processes (preventing cmd.exe/powershell.exe spawned by Word/Excel macros)
options.C: Block credential stealing from the Windows local security authority subsystem
options.E: This is a standard feature of most antivirus software

questions.explanation: The ASR rule 'Block Office applications from creating child processes' (GUID: D4F940AB-401B-4EFC-AADC-AD5F3C50688A) prevents Word, Excel, and PowerPoint from spawning cmd.exe, powershell.exe, or wscript.exe — the typical chain used by malicious macros to deliver payloads.

questions.question: A standard user on a locked-down Windows desktop finds that wmic.exe is not blocked by AppLocker. How can they abuse this?

options.A: wmic.exe cannot be used for offensive purposes on modern Windows
options.B: wmic.exe process call create 'cmd.exe' can spawn processes (including cmd.exe or PowerShell) as a LOLBin AppLocker bypass
options.C: wmic.exe can be used to bypass BitLocker drive encryption
options.D: wmic.exe can dump LSASS memory for credential extraction
options.E: Only during the initial scoping meeting

questions.explanation: wmic.exe process call create executes arbitrary processes through WMI. As a signed Microsoft binary, it is allowed by many AppLocker policies. Attackers use it to spawn cmd.exe, run PowerShell, or execute other payloads, bypassing application whitelisting.

questions.question: What is the purpose of Microsoft's 'Attack Surface Reduction' (ASR) rules as part of a desktop lockdown strategy?

options.A: To reduce the number of open network ports on workstations
options.B: A set of configurable rules in Microsoft Defender that block specific high-risk behaviours (e.g., Office macros spawning shells, credential theft, ransomware patterns) independent of signature-based AV detection
options.C: To limit the number of installed applications on each workstation
options.D: To restrict USB device access and removable media
options.E: This is not applicable to web application testing

questions.explanation: ASR rules block specific behaviours commonly observed in malware — macro-spawned processes, Office injecting into other processes, credential theft from LSASS, persistence via WMI subscriptions — providing behavioural protection that works even against previously unseen malware.

questions.question: When testing a locked-down Windows desktop, a tester finds PowerShell is in Constrained Language Mode. What does this restrict?

options.A: PowerShell can only run scripts shorter than 1000 lines
options.B: PowerShell blocks .NET type access, COM objects, and many API calls that enable advanced attacks, significantly limiting post-exploitation capabilities
options.C: PowerShell cannot connect to remote systems via WinRM
options.D: PowerShell scripts cannot be longer than 1MB in size
options.E: Only if requested by the third-party hosting provider

questions.explanation: Constrained Language Mode (CLM) restricts PowerShell to basic operations — it blocks access to .NET types, COM objects, direct API calls, and advanced features used by offensive tools (Invoke-Mimikatz, PowerView). It is enforced automatically by WDAC policies and significantly raises the bar for attackers.

questions.question: Which Windows security feature encrypts the contents of a specific folder (rather than the whole drive) using the logged-in user's credentials, and is transparent to the user?

options.B: EFS (Encrypting File System)
options.E: This is a requirement of the GDPR only

questions.explanation: EFS encrypts individual files and folders using the current user's certificate. The encryption is transparent when the user is logged in but protects files if the drive is accessed offline or by another OS account. Attackers target the EFS certificate (stored in DPAPI) to decrypt EFS-protected files.

questions.question: A hardened Windows build blocks execution of unsigned scripts via PowerShell execution policy. A tester bypasses this with: powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File script.ps1. What does this demonstrate?

options.A: A vulnerability in PowerShell's cryptographic signature verification
options.B: Execution policy is not a security boundary — it is a user convenience feature easily bypassed with command-line flags or by piping script content to powershell.exe; only WDAC or AppLocker prevent unsigned script execution
options.C: That PowerShell must be uninstalled on locked-down systems
options.D: A UAC bypass that elevates the script to administrator privileges
options.E: Only when performing a white-box test

questions.explanation: PowerShell execution policy (Restricted, AllSigned, RemoteSigned, etc.) is not a security control — it can be trivially bypassed. Only WDAC script enforcement or AppLocker script rules (using SRP-based enforcement) can actually prevent unsigned PowerShell scripts from running.

questions.question: What is 'business email compromise' (BEC) and why is it particularly difficult to detect?

options.A: Malware delivered via a business email attachment that compromises the recipient's machine
options.B: A fraud where attackers impersonate executives or business partners via spoofed or compromised email accounts to authorise fraudulent payments or data disclosures — it contains no malware, bypassing technical email filters
options.C: Mass phishing targeting business email accounts with credential-stealing links
options.D: Compromising a business email server to intercept all internal communications
options.E: This is handled by the ISP

questions.explanation: BEC relies on social deception rather than malware. Emails impersonate the CEO, CFO, or a trusted supplier requesting urgent wire transfers or invoice changes. Because there are no malicious links or attachments, BEC often bypasses email security gateways and AV scanning.

questions.question: An attacker registers the domain 'paypa1.com' (with a number 1 instead of letter l) to conduct phishing. What is this technique called?

options.B: Typosquatting
options.E: Only if the tester has a valid security clearance

questions.explanation: Typosquatting registers domains that are common misspellings or visual substitutions of legitimate domains. Combined with a convincing clone of the real website, it captures credentials from users who mistype or are deceived by the similar-looking domain name.

questions.question: What is a 'homograph attack' in the context of phishing?

options.A: Sending identical phishing emails to a large group of people simultaneously
options.B: Using Unicode characters that look visually identical (or very similar) to ASCII characters to register deceptive domain names (e.g., using Cyrillic 'а' instead of Latin 'a')
options.C: Cloning a legitimate website's HTML and CSS exactly
options.D: Using the same email template as a previous legitimate communication
options.E: This is not a standard part of the penetration testing lifecycle

questions.explanation: Homograph (or IDN homograph) attacks exploit Unicode internationalised domain names where characters from different scripts look identical. For example, 'аpple.com' using Cyrillic 'а' (U+0430) is visually indistinguishable from 'apple.com' but is a completely different domain.

questions.question: Which social engineering countermeasure specifically addresses the risk of vishing (voice phishing) attacks on a helpdesk?

options.A: Deploying email filtering with DKIM and SPF
options.B: Implementing a callback procedure: hang up and call back the requester using a number from the official directory, never the number provided by the caller
options.C: Requiring all password resets to be submitted via the self-service portal
options.D: Training staff not to answer calls from unknown numbers
options.E: Only after the final report has been delivered

questions.explanation: The callback procedure defeats vishing by breaking the attacker's communication channel. Even if an attacker spoofs the caller ID, calling back via an independently verified number (from the staff directory, not from the caller) ensures communication is with the legitimate person.

questions.question: An attacker harvests information from LinkedIn, company websites, and job postings before a phishing engagement. Which category of information is MOST valuable for crafting a convincing spear-phish?

options.B: Employee names, roles, reporting lines, current projects, technology stack (from job postings), and the email naming convention (e.g., first.last@company.com)
options.C: The office building's street address and CCTV positions
options.D: The company's IT vendor list from their website's privacy policy
options.E: This is a requirement of the ISO 27001 standard

questions.explanation: Employee names, hierarchies, and current projects enable highly personalised and credible spear-phishing lures. The email naming convention from visible addresses or LinkedIn allows constructing valid email addresses for targeted employees. Technology stack from job postings helps craft IT-related pretexts.

questions.question: What is the 'authority' principle in Cialdini's influence framework, and how do attackers exploit it?

options.A: People comply with requests from people they are attracted to; attackers use flattery
options.B: People tend to comply with requests from perceived authority figures (managers, IT, police, auditors); attackers impersonate these roles to lower resistance to unusual requests
options.C: People comply with requests when they feel they owe something; attackers offer small gifts before making requests
options.D: People follow the behaviour of their peers; attackers claim everyone else has already complied
options.E: None of the above

questions.explanation: The authority principle exploits the ingrained tendency to obey perceived authority figures. Attackers impersonate senior management, IT security, regulators, or law enforcement to make targets comply with requests they would otherwise refuse (password disclosure, clicking links, granting access).

questions.question: During a red team engagement, an operator calls an employee and says 'I'm from IT security, we've detected suspicious activity on your account and need you to install a remote access tool immediately to investigate.' Which defence would most effectively stop this?

options.A: Email filtering that blocks executable attachments
options.B: Security awareness training that teaches staff IT will never call asking them to install software, combined with a verification procedure (call back via the official IT number to confirm)
options.C: Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) that blocks remote access tools
options.E: All of the above

questions.explanation: Technical controls (EDR, MFA) help but don't prevent the initial social engineering step. Training staff with specific 'tells' (IT never requests remote access via unsolicited calls) and a call-back verification procedure addresses the human vulnerability directly.

questions.question: What is 'open source intelligence' (OSINT) and name two tools used for corporate OSINT?

options.A: Proprietary intelligence purchased from commercial providers; tools: Mandiant, Recorded Future
options.B: Intelligence gathered from publicly available sources including websites, social media, DNS, and public filings; tools include theHarvester (email/domain enumeration) and Maltego (relationship mapping)
options.C: Intelligence gathered from scanning target IP ranges; tools: Nmap and Shodan
options.D: Intelligence gathered from human sources; tools: LinkedIn and Facebook
options.E: Only after formal approval from the board of directors

questions.explanation: OSINT uses publicly available information — no hacking required. For corporate targets, theHarvester collects emails, subdomains, and employee names; Maltego visualises entity relationships. Other OSINT sources include LinkedIn, Shodan (internet-facing assets), WHOIS, Certificate Transparency logs, and GitHub.

questions.question: A social engineering assessment report finds that 40% of employees clicked a phishing link. What metric should be tracked over time to measure the effectiveness of security awareness training?

options.A: The total number of phishing emails blocked by the email gateway
options.B: The click-through rate on simulated phishing campaigns over successive monthly or quarterly campaigns, tracking whether the rate decreases after training
options.C: The number of employees who completed the mandatory security awareness e-learning module
options.D: The score on the annual security policy knowledge quiz
options.E: This is not a requirement for CREST certification

questions.explanation: Click-through rates on simulated phishing are the most direct behavioural metric for security awareness. Completion rates for training courses measure exposure, not behaviour change. Tracking click rates before and after targeted training shows whether training actually changes employee behaviour.

questions.question: An attacker on a guest VM exploits a vulnerability that allows them to write to host memory outside the VM's allocated range. What class of attack is this?

options.A: A privilege escalation attack within the guest OS
options.B: A VM escape / hypervisor breakout — the guest crosses the isolation boundary to affect the host or other VMs
options.C: A denial-of-service attack against the hypervisor scheduler
options.D: A side-channel attack leaking host memory contents to the guest
options.E: It depends on the specific country's jurisdiction

questions.explanation: VM escape exploits vulnerabilities in the hypervisor or virtualised device emulation (e.g., VENOM in QEMU's floppy controller) to break out of the guest sandbox and execute code in the host context, compromising all VMs on that host.

questions.question: What is the purpose of virtualisation-based security (VBS) in Windows, and how does it use the hypervisor?

options.A: VBS uses the hypervisor to sandbox untrusted applications in isolated VMs automatically
options.B: VBS uses the Hyper-V hypervisor to create an isolated secure world (Virtual Secure Mode) that protects sensitive data — such as LSASS credentials via Credential Guard — even from a compromised kernel
options.C: VBS uses virtualisation to snapshot the OS state for quick recovery after a ransomware attack
options.D: VBS uses the hypervisor to enforce AppLocker policies at the hardware level
options.E: Only when using automated scanning tools

questions.explanation: VBS runs the Windows kernel in a less-privileged VM and places sensitive security components (Credential Guard, HVCI) in a separate, more-privileged Virtual Secure Mode. Even if the OS kernel is compromised, attackers cannot extract LSASS credentials because they are stored in the isolated VSM world.

questions.question: A type-1 (bare-metal) hypervisor differs from a type-2 hypervisor in which key way that affects security?

options.A: Type-1 hypervisors can only run Windows VMs; type-2 can run any OS
options.B: Type-1 runs directly on hardware with no host OS layer (smaller attack surface); type-2 runs on top of a host OS, meaning a compromised host OS can compromise all guest VMs
options.C: Type-1 hypervisors do not support snapshots; type-2 do
options.D: Type-2 hypervisors are always more performant than type-1
options.E: This is handled by the client's internal IT department

questions.explanation: Type-1 hypervisors (VMware ESXi, Xen, Hyper-V) have a smaller attack surface with no general-purpose host OS beneath them. Type-2 hypervisors (VMware Workstation, VirtualBox) rely on the host OS, so any kernel compromise in the host can affect all VMs.

questions.question: What is a 'snapshot revert' security risk in virtualised environments used for security testing?

options.A: Reverting a snapshot can introduce unpatched vulnerabilities by rolling back to an older, unpatched OS state
options.B: Snapshot revert encrypts all data on the VM, causing data loss
options.C: Reverting a snapshot increases VM CPU utilisation to 100%
options.D: Snapshot revert exposes the VM to other hypervisor tenants
options.E: During the post-engagement debrief session

questions.explanation: Reverting to an old snapshot restores the VM to its state at snapshot time — including unpatched software, expired certificates, revoked credentials, or previously-disabled security features. This can re-introduce vulnerabilities that were subsequently patched.

questions.question: In VMware ESXi environments, what is the risk of leaving the ESXi Shell and SSH access enabled on hypervisor hosts?

options.A: It has no security impact — ESXi is a hypervisor, not a general-purpose OS
options.B: ESXi Shell and SSH provide direct hypervisor command-line access; if compromised (via credential theft or brute force), an attacker has full control over all hosted VMs, VM files, and the host network
options.C: Enabling SSH on ESXi disables vSphere High Availability (HA) automatically
options.D: The ESXi Shell exposes management traffic to guest VM network interfaces
options.E: Only if the vulnerability is classified as Critical

questions.explanation: ESXi Shell and SSH give root-level access to the hypervisor itself — not just a guest. An attacker with ESXi root access can power off, clone, or exfiltrate all VMs, access VM disks directly, capture VM memory (including running credentials), and pivot to the management network.

questions.question: macOS Gatekeeper prevents unsigned applications from running. What is the standard technique to bypass Gatekeeper when distributing a malicious application?

options.A: Exploit a kernel vulnerability to disable Gatekeeper system-wide
options.B: Obtain an Apple developer certificate (free or paid), sign the application, optionally notarise it with Apple — or socially engineer the user into right-click > Open to bypass the quarantine check
options.C: Modify the /etc/gatekeeper.conf file to add an exception
options.D: Install a malicious kernel extension to disable code signing checks
options.E: This is a standard feature of most antivirus software

questions.explanation: The most practical bypass for most attacks is obtaining a legitimate (or stolen) Apple developer certificate to sign the payload, or tricking users into using right-click > Open which bypasses the Gatekeeper block. The quarantine attribute (com.apple.quarantine) applied to downloaded files triggers Gatekeeper; files received through non-browser methods (AirDrop, etc.) may not get this attribute.

questions.question: What is Transparency, Consent and Control (TCC) on macOS and how do attackers attempt to bypass it?

options.A: TCC is Apple's App Store review process; attackers submit malicious apps that pass review
options.B: TCC is a macOS privacy framework requiring user consent before apps can access Camera, Microphone, Contacts, Location, and full disk. Attackers bypass it by injecting into TCC-approved processes (e.g., Finder, Terminal) or exploiting vulnerabilities that reset TCC databases
options.C: TCC is the macOS firewall component; attackers bypass it with kernel exploits
options.D: TCC controls code signing; attackers bypass it by stripping the code signature from binaries
options.E: Only during the initial scoping meeting

questions.explanation: TCC enforces user-consent gates on sensitive resources. A common bypass is to inject code into a process that already has TCC permissions (e.g., inject into Terminal which has full disk access). Historical TCC bypasses include direct database manipulation (before SIP protected it) and exploiting migration tools.

questions.question: What does System Integrity Protection (SIP) on macOS protect, and what are the limits of this protection?

options.A: SIP encrypts all user data on the system volume; it does not protect system binaries
options.B: SIP prevents modification of core OS directories (/System, /usr, /bin, /sbin) and system processes even by root; however, it does not protect user directories, third-party software, or network traffic
options.C: SIP is a firewall that prevents unauthorised inbound connections to system services
options.D: SIP prevents applications from running without a valid Apple notarisation ticket
options.E: This is not applicable to web application testing

questions.explanation: SIP (rootless mode) restricts even root from modifying protected OS paths, loading unsigned kernel extensions, or attaching to system processes with a debugger. It does not protect user home directories, /Applications (third-party), or application data — so malware can still persist in LaunchAgents and user directories.

questions.question: An attacker wants to persist on a compromised macOS system without root. Which persistence mechanism is available to standard user accounts?

options.B: Adding a LaunchAgent plist to ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ — this runs automatically at login for the user without requiring any elevated privileges
options.D: Installing a kernel extension in /Library/Extensions/ (requires root and SIP bypass)
options.E: Only if requested by the third-party hosting provider

questions.explanation: ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ is writable by the user and any plist placed there is executed by launchd at login. It is the standard user-level persistence location for macOS malware, analogous to HKCU\Run in Windows. LaunchDaemons require root and run as root at boot.

questions.question: What is the macOS Keychain and what attack technique targets it during a post-exploitation engagement?

options.A: Keychain is the macOS update mechanism; attackers manipulate it to prevent security updates
options.B: Keychain is the macOS credential store for passwords, certificates, and private keys. Post-exploitation, attackers use security dump-keychain or tools like Chainbreaker to extract stored credentials — the user's login password often unlocks the login keychain
options.C: Keychain is the macOS firewall rule database; attackers modify it to allow reverse shells
options.D: Keychain stores FileVault encryption keys; attackers extract it to decrypt the disk offline
options.E: This is a requirement of the GDPR only

questions.explanation: The macOS Keychain stores Wi-Fi passwords, website credentials, certificates, and application secrets. Tools like `security dump-keychain -d` (when run in the user's session context) or Chainbreaker can extract credentials. Many keychain items are unlocked when the user logs in, making post-exploitation keychain dumping very productive.

questions.question: What is 'tailgating' (also called 'piggybacking') and what is the most effective control to prevent it?

options.A: Following a target vehicle into a secured car park; prevented by ANPR (Automatic Number Plate Recognition)
options.B: Following an authorised person through a secured door without presenting credentials yourself; best prevented by mantrap/airlock entry systems with single-person detection (one person per authentication)
options.C: Intercepting wireless credentials by following an employee home; prevented by WPA3 Enterprise
options.D: Cloning an RFID badge by walking close to someone; prevented by Faraday badge sleeves
options.E: Only when performing a white-box test

questions.explanation: Tailgating exploits social conventions (holding a door open) to bypass physical access controls. Mantrap/airlock doors — where only one person can enter per badge swipe — are the most effective technical control. Staff training to challenge tailgaters also helps but relies on human compliance.

questions.question: An attacker successfully reads an employee's HID Prox Card from 30cm away using a commercially available reader. What class of attack is this and how is it mitigated?

options.A: A relay attack; mitigated by distance-bounding protocols
options.B: An RFID skimming attack against low-frequency (125kHz) proximity cards which transmit credentials without encryption; mitigated by upgrading to MIFARE DESFire or similar high-frequency encrypted smart cards (13.56MHz) and using Faraday shielding sleeves
options.C: A brute-force attack against the card's PIN; mitigated by increasing PIN complexity
options.D: A man-in-the-middle attack; mitigated by certificate pinning on the card reader
options.E: This is handled by the ISP

questions.explanation: HID Prox and EM4100 proximity cards broadcast their card number in cleartext with no authentication or encryption. Tools like the Proxmark can read and clone these cards from short distances. The mitigation is replacing them with cryptographically authenticated smart cards (MIFARE DESFire EV2/EV3, iCLASS Seos).

questions.question: What is a 'rubber ducky' style attack in the context of physical security testing?

options.A: Using a squeaky toy to distract security guards
options.B: Inserting a device (USB Rubber Ducky, Bash Bunny) that masquerades as a USB keyboard and automatically types a pre-programmed payload at high speed when plugged in, bypassing application whitelisting that only blocks executables
options.C: Planting a Wi-Fi pineapple in a rubber duck decoy to conduct wireless attacks
options.D: A social engineering technique where an attacker pretends to be a helpless visitor to gain entry
options.E: Only if the tester has a valid security clearance

questions.explanation: HID-emulation attacks (USB Rubber Ducky, Bash Bunny in HID mode) present as a standard keyboard. The OS trusts keyboard input implicitly, so the device types commands at superhuman speed (opening PowerShell, running a payload) in seconds. Mitigations include USB device management policies, port blocking, and disabling AutoRun/AutoPlay.

questions.question: During a physical penetration test, a tester photographs the underside of keyboards and the area under monitors. What are they looking for?

options.A: Evidence of USB keyloggers attached between the keyboard cable and the PC
options.B: Passwords written on sticky notes — a common finding that can give immediate access to systems without any technical attack
options.C: MAC addresses written on equipment labels
options.E: This is not a standard part of the penetration testing lifecycle

questions.explanation: Written credentials are one of the most common findings in physical security assessments. Employees write passwords on sticky notes attached to monitors, keyboards, or stored in unlocked drawers. These immediately compromise accounts without any technical exploitation. The finding demonstrates that password complexity requirements drive users toward insecure storage.

questions.question: What is 'lock picking' in the context of a physical penetration test and what is its legal and ethical requirement before conducting it?

options.A: Lock picking is illegal in all jurisdictions and should never be included in a penetration test
options.B: Lock picking involves manipulating lock mechanisms (using picks, tension wrenches, bump keys, or bypass tools) to open locked doors without the key. It requires explicit written authorisation covering the specific locks and locations to be tested, before any attempt is made
options.C: Lock picking refers to social engineering a locksmith to grant access, requiring no special authorisation
options.D: Lock picking is only legal if conducted by a licensed locksmith and so the penetration tester must hold a locksmith qualification
options.E: Only after the final report has been delivered

questions.explanation: Physical penetration testing techniques including lock picking require explicit, written authorisation that clearly defines scope (which buildings, which locks, what hours). Without this, the activity constitutes criminal damage or breaking and entering. Legal requirements vary by jurisdiction — some countries restrict lock-pick tool possession itself.

questions.question: What security risk arises from running a Docker container with the --privileged flag?

options.A: The container can only be accessed by root on the host
options.B: The --privileged flag disables all Linux namespace and capability isolation, giving the container full access to host devices and kernel features — effectively the same as root on the host, enabling a trivial container escape
options.C: The container is restricted to using 100% of one CPU core
options.D: The --privileged flag exposes container ports directly to the internet
options.E: This is a requirement of the ISO 27001 standard

questions.explanation: A privileged container has access to all host devices (/dev), can load kernel modules, and has every Linux capability enabled. Escape is trivial: mount the host filesystem via /dev/sda, write a cron job or SSH key, and exit the container. Containers should run with minimal capabilities (--cap-drop ALL, --cap-add only what is needed).

questions.question: An attacker compromises a container and finds that the Docker socket (/var/run/docker.sock) is mounted inside it. How can this be exploited?

options.A: The attacker can only stop and restart containers, not escape to the host
options.B: The Docker socket gives the container control of the Docker daemon on the host. The attacker runs a new privileged container mounting the host filesystem, chroots into it, and achieves full host root access — a complete container escape
options.C: Mounting the Docker socket allows the container to pull images from Docker Hub only
options.D: The attacker can read other container logs but cannot modify the host
options.E: None of the above

questions.explanation: Mounting the Docker socket inside a container is equivalent to giving it root on the host. The container can issue Docker API commands to start new privileged containers, mount /host-root into them, then chroot out of the container to interact with the full host OS. This is a common misconfiguration in CI/CD pipelines and monitoring agents.

questions.question: What is a 'distroless' container image and what security benefit does it provide?

options.A: A container image with no operating system at all, used only for data storage
options.B: A minimal container image containing only the application and its runtime dependencies — no shell, package manager, or debug tools. This significantly reduces the attack surface because attackers cannot use common post-exploitation tools even if they achieve code execution
options.C: A container image that automatically removes itself after the container stops
options.D: A container image built without any Linux distribution branding, indistinguishable from other distributions
options.E: All of the above

questions.explanation: Distroless images (popularised by Google) omit shells (/bin/sh), package managers (apt, apk), and other OS utilities. Post-exploitation activities that rely on bash, curl, wget, or package installation are blocked. Combined with read-only filesystems and no-new-privileges flags, distroless images significantly harden container deployments.

questions.question: What is a 'software supply chain attack' and which high-profile incident demonstrated its risk?

options.A: An attack on the physical logistics chain delivering hardware components; demonstrated by the Bloomberg Supermicro hardware implant claims
options.B: Compromising a software vendor, build system, or dependency so that malicious code is distributed to downstream users through a trusted update mechanism; demonstrated by the SolarWinds Orion compromise (SUNBURST backdoor, 2020)
options.C: Exploiting weak supplier contracts to access customer data; demonstrated by the Target HVAC vendor breach
options.D: Attacking the software escrow service holding source code for critical infrastructure
options.E: Only after formal approval from the board of directors

questions.explanation: In the SolarWinds attack, threat actors compromised the build pipeline and injected the SUNBURST backdoor into legitimate Orion software updates, signed with SolarWinds' own certificate. 18,000 organisations installed the trojanised update. This exemplifies supply chain attacks: the distribution mechanism itself is weaponised.

questions.question: What is the purpose of SAST (Static Application Security Testing) and at which stage of the SDLC should it be applied?

options.A: SAST analyses running applications by sending malicious inputs; applied in production during staging
options.B: SAST analyses source code or compiled bytecode without executing it, detecting vulnerabilities (SQL injection patterns, hardcoded secrets, unsafe functions) at development or CI/CD pipeline stage — 'shift left' before code reaches production
options.C: SAST tests the application's security headers by making HTTP requests; applied pre-release
options.D: SAST monitors production application logs for attack patterns; applied continuously in production
options.E: This is not a requirement for CREST certification

questions.explanation: SAST is a 'white-box' technique that inspects source code, bytecode, or binary without executing it. It is most valuable when integrated into CI/CD pipelines so developers get security feedback on every commit — the 'shift left' security principle. Tools include Semgrep, SonarQube, Checkmarx, and Bandit (Python).

questions.question: A developer accidentally commits an AWS access key to a public GitHub repository. What should be the FIRST action taken, and why?

options.A: Use git rebase to remove the commit from history — this is sufficient because the commit is removed
options.B: Immediately revoke/rotate the AWS key in the AWS console — the key should be treated as fully compromised because automated scanners (GitGuardian, truffleHog bots) detect and harvest secrets from public commits within seconds of publication
options.C: Make the repository private immediately — this prevents any further exposure
options.D: Open a GitHub support ticket to have the commit removed from GitHub's servers
options.E: It depends on the specific country's jurisdiction

questions.explanation: Automated secret-harvesting bots scan public GitHub pushes in real time. Even if the commit is deleted or the repo made private within minutes, the secret must be assumed compromised and revoked immediately. Git history rewriting is secondary — the revocation/rotation is the critical first step.

questions.question: During a penetration test, you need to identify the registrar, name servers, and registration dates for a target domain. Which protocol is specifically designed for querying domain registration databases?

options.B: WHOIS
options.E: Only when using automated scanning tools

questions.explanation: WHOIS is the traditional protocol (port 43) used to query registrar databases for domain registration information including registrar, name servers, dates, and registrant details. While RDAP is its modern successor, WHOIS remains the most widely referenced protocol for this purpose.

questions.question: A penetration tester discovers that a target domain's WHOIS record shows registrant contact details replaced with a third-party privacy service address. What is the most likely reason for this?

options.A: The domain has expired and is in a redemption grace period
options.B: The registrar has applied WHOIS privacy/proxy protection to hide the true registrant
options.C: The domain is using DNSSEC which encrypts WHOIS records
options.D: The domain is hosted behind a CDN which masks registration data
options.E: This is handled by the client's internal IT department

questions.explanation: WHOIS privacy or proxy services replace the true registrant's contact information with that of the privacy service provider. This is a common feature offered by registrars to protect the registrant's personal data from public WHOIS lookups.

questions.question: You want to discover what a target company's website looked like three years ago and identify domains or infrastructure that may have since been removed. Which resource is most appropriate?

options.B: VirusTotal domain lookup
options.E: During the post-engagement debrief session

questions.explanation: The Wayback Machine archives historical snapshots of websites over time, allowing a tester to review previous versions of a target site, discover removed content, old infrastructure references, and previously exposed information.

questions.question: During reconnaissance, a tester wants to identify all domains registered by the same organisation. Which WHOIS technique is most effective for this when privacy protection is not in use?

options.A: Performing a reverse WHOIS lookup by registrant name or email
options.B: Querying the target's MX records for related domains
options.C: Brute-forcing subdomains of the known domain
options.D: Checking the target's SSL certificate SAN field
options.E: Only if the vulnerability is classified as Critical

questions.explanation: A reverse WHOIS lookup searches registration databases by registrant name, email, or organisation, revealing all domains registered by the same entity. This is a powerful technique for mapping an organisation's full domain portfolio when privacy protection is absent.

questions.question: Which of the following domain registration statuses indicates that a domain is locked at the registry level and cannot be transferred, deleted, or have its name servers changed without the lock being removed?

options.B: serverDeleteProhibited
options.E: This is a standard feature of most antivirus software

questions.explanation: Server-level locks (serverTransferProhibited, serverUpdateProhibited, serverDeleteProhibited) are set by the registry and provide the strongest protection. When both serverTransferProhibited and serverUpdateProhibited are active, the domain cannot be transferred or have its name servers changed without the registry removing the locks.

questions.question: ICANN introduced RDAP as a replacement for the traditional WHOIS protocol. Which advantage does RDAP offer over WHOIS from a reconnaissance perspective?

options.A: RDAP bypasses domain privacy protections automatically
options.B: RDAP returns structured JSON responses with standardised data formats
options.C: RDAP queries are anonymous and cannot be rate-limited
options.D: RDAP provides access to the registrant's payment information
options.E: Only during the initial scoping meeting

questions.explanation: RDAP (Registration Data Access Protocol) returns data in a standardised JSON format over HTTPS, making it easier to parse programmatically compared to the free-text format of traditional WHOIS responses. It does not bypass privacy protections or provide payment data.

questions.question: A penetration tester attempts an AXFR request against a target's authoritative name server and receives a full copy of the DNS zone. What has the tester successfully performed?

options.B: A DNS zone transfer
options.E: This is not applicable to web application testing

questions.explanation: AXFR is the DNS zone transfer mechanism. When an authoritative name server is misconfigured to allow AXFR requests from any source, an attacker can retrieve the entire zone file, revealing all DNS records including internal hostnames and IP addresses.

questions.question: Which DNS record type would a penetration tester query to identify the mail servers responsible for accepting email on behalf of the target domain?

options.B: CNAME record
options.E: Only if requested by the third-party hosting provider

questions.explanation: MX (Mail Exchange) records specify the mail servers responsible for receiving email for a domain. Querying MX records reveals email infrastructure which may include hostnames that expose internal naming conventions or third-party email services.

questions.question: During DNS enumeration, a tester uses 'dig target.com ANY' but receives a minimal response. What is the most likely explanation?

options.B: Many modern DNS servers and resolvers refuse or limit ANY queries (RFC 8482)
options.C: The dig tool does not support the ANY query type
options.D: The domain is using DNSSEC which blocks ANY queries
options.E: This is a requirement of the GDPR only

questions.explanation: RFC 8482 allows DNS servers to minimally respond to ANY queries, and many modern authoritative servers and resolvers now refuse to return all records for such queries to reduce abuse potential. Testers should query specific record types (A, AAAA, MX, TXT, etc.) individually.

questions.question: A penetration tester discovers a TXT record containing 'v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ~all' on the target domain. What does this reveal about the target's infrastructure?

options.A: The domain is hosted on Google Cloud Platform
options.B: The organisation uses Google Workspace (Gmail) for their email
options.C: The domain's DNS is managed by Google
options.D: The organisation's web application uses Google OAuth exclusively
options.E: Only when performing a white-box test

questions.explanation: An SPF record that includes _spf.google.com indicates that Google's mail servers are authorised to send email on behalf of the domain, strongly suggesting the organisation uses Google Workspace (formerly G Suite) for their email services.

questions.question: Which tool is specifically designed for DNS enumeration and can perform zone transfers, brute-force subdomain discovery, and reverse lookups in a single assessment?

options.B: DNSRecon
options.E: This is handled by the ISP

questions.explanation: DNSRecon is a purpose-built DNS enumeration tool that supports zone transfers (AXFR), brute-force subdomain enumeration, reverse lookups, Google dork-based enumeration, cache snooping, and DNS record enumeration — all from a single tool.

questions.question: During passive DNS reconnaissance, a tester uses a service that aggregates historical DNS resolution data to find subdomains that no longer have active DNS records. Which type of service is being used?

options.B: A passive DNS database (e.g., SecurityTrails, Farsight DNSDB)
options.E: Only if the tester has a valid security clearance

questions.explanation: Passive DNS databases collect and store historical DNS resolution data from sensors distributed across the internet. They allow testers to discover subdomains and IP address mappings that may no longer exist in live DNS, revealing historical infrastructure.

questions.question: A penetration tester reviews the target's robots.txt file and finds 'Disallow: /admin-portal/' and 'Disallow: /internal-api/'. Why is this finding significant for reconnaissance?

options.A: These paths are guaranteed to be protected by authentication
options.B: The robots.txt reveals paths the organisation wants hidden from search engines, which may be sensitive attack surfaces
options.C: The disallow directive prevents any HTTP client from accessing these paths
options.D: The robots.txt confirms these directories contain known vulnerabilities
options.E: This is not a standard part of the penetration testing lifecycle

questions.explanation: robots.txt is a voluntary directive for well-behaved web crawlers. From a security perspective, entries in Disallow often reveal sensitive directories, admin panels, or API endpoints that the organisation does not want publicly indexed — making them high-value targets for further investigation.

questions.question: While analysing a target website, a tester uses Wappalyzer and identifies that the site is running WordPress 5.8 with the WooCommerce plugin. How should this information be used in the engagement?

options.A: It is irrelevant; only server-side vulnerabilities matter
options.B: The specific versions should be checked against CVE databases for known vulnerabilities, and WordPress/plugin-specific enumeration tools should be employed
options.C: The tester should immediately attempt default WordPress credentials
options.D: The tester should report this as a critical finding because WordPress is inherently insecure
options.E: Only after the final report has been delivered

questions.explanation: Identifying specific CMS versions and plugins allows the tester to search for known CVEs, use specialised tools like WPScan for deeper enumeration, and understand the attack surface. Version identification is a key step before moving to vulnerability analysis.

questions.question: Which HTTP response header can reveal the underlying web server software and version during website reconnaissance?

options.B: Server
options.E: This is a requirement of the ISO 27001 standard

questions.explanation: The 'Server' HTTP response header typically reveals the web server software and sometimes its version (e.g., 'Apache/2.4.51' or 'nginx/1.21.3'). This information assists in identifying known vulnerabilities for the specific server version.

questions.question: A penetration tester wants to map the full directory structure and linked resources of a target website without using a vulnerability scanner. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Manually browsing the site and taking screenshots
options.B: Using a web spider/crawler such as wget --mirror or Burp Suite's crawler to recursively follow links and map the site structure
options.C: Running an Nmap scan against port 80 and 443
options.E: None of the above

questions.explanation: Web spidering/crawling tools recursively follow links from a starting page to map the full site structure, discover linked resources, and identify content. Burp Suite's crawler and wget with mirroring options are commonly used for this purpose during web reconnaissance.

questions.question: During website analysis, a tester discovers a sitemap.xml file. Which of the following best describes the reconnaissance value of this file?

options.A: It contains the site's database schema
options.B: It provides a structured list of URLs the site owner wants indexed, potentially revealing hidden or less obvious pages
options.C: It lists all users who have accounts on the website
options.D: It shows real-time server performance metrics
options.E: All of the above

questions.explanation: sitemap.xml is intended to help search engines discover pages. For a penetration tester, it provides a comprehensive map of URL paths the site owner wants indexed, which may include pages not easily found through browsing — such as staging environments, old content, or rarely linked sections.

questions.question: A tester examines the HTML source of a target web application and discovers comments containing developer names, internal server IPs, and TODO notes about unpatched features. What category does this finding fall under?

options.B: Information disclosure through HTML source code comments
options.E: Only after formal approval from the board of directors

questions.explanation: HTML comments left by developers that reveal internal infrastructure details, employee names, or unpatched features constitute information disclosure. This is a common finding during web site analysis that aids further attack planning.

questions.question: Which Google dork would most effectively help a penetration tester find publicly accessible directory listings on a target domain?

options.B: site:target.com intitle:"index of" inurl:/
options.E: This is not a requirement for CREST certification

questions.explanation: The dork 'site:target.com intitle:"index of"' searches for Apache/Nginx directory listing pages on the target domain. These listings expose file and folder structures and can reveal sensitive files that were not intended to be publicly accessible.

questions.question: A penetration tester wants to find exposed configuration files on a target's web infrastructure using Google. Which search query is most likely to yield results?

options.A: site:target.com filetype:conf OR filetype:cfg OR filetype:env
options.B: site:target.com inurl:https
options.E: It depends on the specific country's jurisdiction

questions.explanation: Using 'filetype:' operators combined with 'site:' allows a tester to search for specific file extensions that commonly contain configuration data (.conf, .cfg, .env). These files may reveal database credentials, API keys, or internal infrastructure details.

questions.question: Shodan is frequently used during the reconnaissance phase of a penetration test. What does Shodan primarily index?

options.A: Web page content and hyperlinks, similar to Google
options.B: Internet-connected devices and services by scanning ports and capturing banner information
options.C: Social media profiles and public posts
options.E: Only when using automated scanning tools

questions.explanation: Shodan is a search engine that scans the internet for connected devices and services, indexing banner information from open ports. It reveals exposed services, software versions, default configurations, and IoT devices, making it invaluable for infrastructure reconnaissance.

questions.question: A tester uses the Google operator 'cache:target.com/page' during reconnaissance. What is the primary purpose of this technique?

options.A: To bypass the target's WAF and access the live page
options.B: To view Google's cached version of the page, which may contain content that has since been removed or modified
options.C: To inject malicious content into Google's cache
options.D: To perform a denial-of-service attack against Google's cache servers
options.E: This is handled by the client's internal IT department

questions.explanation: Google's cache operator retrieves the last version of a page that Google's crawler indexed. This can reveal content that has been removed or modified, such as previously exposed credentials, employee details, or sensitive documents.

questions.question: Which search engine is specifically designed for finding internet-facing assets using queries based on SSL certificate data, HTTP response content, and network banners?

options.B: Bing
options.E: During the post-engagement debrief session

questions.explanation: Censys is a search engine that indexes internet-wide scan data, including SSL/TLS certificates, HTTP responses, and service banners. It allows testers to search by certificate fields, HTTP body content, or protocol-specific attributes to discover an organisation's internet-facing assets.

questions.question: During Google dorking, a tester uses 'site:target.com -site:www.target.com'. What is the purpose of this query?

options.A: To find pages only on the www subdomain
options.B: To discover indexed pages on subdomains other than www, potentially revealing staging, development, or internal systems
options.C: To remove the target domain from Google's index
options.D: To check if the www subdomain has been compromised
options.E: Only if the vulnerability is classified as Critical

questions.explanation: This query finds pages indexed under target.com but excludes the main www subdomain, surfacing content on other subdomains such as dev., staging., mail., or vpn. — which may expose less-hardened systems or internal infrastructure.

questions.question: During OSINT gathering, a penetration tester discovers that a target organisation's system administrator has been posting detailed questions about their firewall configuration on a public technical mailing list. Why is this significant?

options.A: It proves the administrator is incompetent and should be fired
options.B: The posts may reveal specific firewall products, software versions, network topology, and configuration weaknesses
options.C: Mailing list posts are encrypted and cannot be read by unauthorised parties
options.D: It confirms the organisation does not have a firewall
options.E: This is a standard feature of most antivirus software

questions.explanation: Technical questions posted publicly by IT staff can inadvertently reveal specific products in use, software versions, configuration challenges, and network architecture details — all of which are valuable intelligence for planning an attack.

questions.question: Which protocol was traditionally used to access Usenet newsgroups, and on which default port does it operate?

options.B: NNTP on port 119
options.E: Only during the initial scoping meeting

questions.explanation: NNTP (Network News Transfer Protocol) operates on port 119 (or 563 for NNTPS) and is the protocol designed for reading and posting articles to Usenet newsgroups. Historical newsgroup posts can contain valuable reconnaissance data.

questions.question: A penetration tester is researching a target organisation and finds archived posts from a developer mailing list where an employee shared a stack trace that includes internal class names, file paths, and database connection strings. What should the tester do?

options.A: Ignore it because mailing list data is considered out of scope
options.B: Document the exposed information as it reveals internal architecture, technology stack, and potentially credentials that can inform subsequent attack phases
options.C: Report the mailing list to the list administrator for removal
options.D: Use the database connection string immediately to access the database
options.E: This is not applicable to web application testing

questions.explanation: Information leaked through mailing lists is valuable OSINT. The tester should document internal architecture details, technology stack information, and any exposed credentials for use in later phases, staying within the agreed scope and rules of engagement.

questions.question: Google Groups archives many public mailing lists and Usenet newsgroups. Which search technique would most effectively find posts by employees of a specific target organisation?

options.A: Searching for 'site:groups.google.com "@target.com"' to find posts from target email addresses
options.B: Searching for 'site:groups.google.com target.com firewall' with no email filter
options.C: Using Shodan to search for NNTP servers at target.com
options.D: Performing a WHOIS lookup on groups.google.com
options.E: Only if requested by the third-party hosting provider

questions.explanation: Searching Google Groups for the target's email domain (e.g., '@target.com') surfaces posts made by employees using their corporate email addresses, often revealing technical details, internal project names, and infrastructure information.

questions.question: During reconnaissance, a tester finds that the target company moderates an open-source project mailing list. Subscribers include several @target.com addresses, and the archive is publicly accessible. What is the primary intelligence value?

options.A: It reveals the company's stock price
options.B: Employee names, email patterns, technical interests, and potentially internal tooling or dependency information
options.E: This is a requirement of the GDPR only

questions.explanation: Public mailing list participation reveals employee identities, the organisation's email format, technical focus areas, and dependencies on specific open-source projects — all useful for social engineering, phishing crafting, and understanding the target's technology stack.

questions.question: A penetration tester discovers a public Mailman list archive for a target's internal security team. The archive shows discussions about an upcoming migration from on-premises Exchange to Microsoft 365. How should this intelligence be classified?

options.A: As irrelevant because it concerns future infrastructure, not current
options.B: As strategic intelligence that reveals the current email platform, planned migration, and a transition period during which security controls may be weakened
options.C: As classified information that the tester cannot legally use
options.D: As a vulnerability that should be exploited immediately
options.E: Only when performing a white-box test

questions.explanation: Migration discussions reveal current infrastructure (Exchange on-premises), future infrastructure (Microsoft 365), timelines, and potentially a period of weakened security posture during the transition. This is strategic intelligence that informs the overall engagement approach.

questions.question: A penetration tester discovers valid corporate credentials for the target organisation on a paste site. Before attempting to use them, what should the tester verify?

options.A: That the paste site is using HTTPS
options.B: That using found credentials is within the agreed scope and rules of engagement for the assessment
options.C: That the credentials were posted within the last 24 hours
options.D: That the credentials belong to a senior executive
options.E: This is handled by the ISP

questions.explanation: The rules of engagement define what actions are authorised. Using credentials found through OSINT may or may not be within scope. The tester must verify with the client or check the scope document before attempting to authenticate with discovered credentials.

questions.question: Which of the following tools is specifically designed to check whether email addresses from a target organisation appear in known data breach databases?

options.B: Have I Been Pwned (HIBP)
options.E: Only if the tester has a valid security clearance

questions.explanation: Have I Been Pwned (HIBP) is a service that aggregates data from known breaches and allows users to check if specific email addresses have been compromised. Penetration testers use it to determine whether target employees' credentials may have been exposed in past breaches.

questions.question: During reconnaissance, a penetration tester finds a public GitHub repository belonging to a target's developer that contains an .env file with database credentials and API keys. What type of information leakage is this?

options.B: Accidental credential exposure through source code repositories
options.E: This is not a standard part of the penetration testing lifecycle

questions.explanation: Accidentally committing sensitive files like .env, configuration files, or private keys to public repositories is a common source of credential exposure. Tools like truffleHog, git-secrets, and GitLeaks are designed to detect such leaks in Git history.

questions.question: A tester wants to search for leaked credentials, configuration files, and sensitive code snippets associated with the target across multiple source code repositories. Which tool automates this process by scanning GitHub for secrets?

options.B: truffleHog
options.E: Only after the final report has been delivered

questions.explanation: truffleHog scans Git repositories for high-entropy strings and known secret patterns (API keys, credentials, tokens) throughout the entire commit history, including previously deleted content. It is a standard tool for detecting information leakage in code repositories.

questions.question: An organisation's AWS S3 bucket is found to be publicly accessible and contains internal documentation, database backups, and customer records. What is the root cause of this information leakage?

options.A: A zero-day vulnerability in AWS S3
options.B: Misconfigured bucket access control policies allowing public read access
options.C: DNS misconfiguration pointing to the S3 bucket
options.D: A man-in-the-middle attack on the AWS API
options.E: This is a requirement of the ISO 27001 standard

questions.explanation: Publicly accessible S3 buckets are a result of misconfigured access control lists (ACLs) or bucket policies that grant read access to 'AllUsers' or 'AuthenticatedUsers'. This is a configuration error, not a vulnerability in the S3 service itself.

questions.question: During an engagement, a penetration tester uses Dehashed and IntelX to search for leaked data associated with the target's domain. What type of intelligence sources are these platforms?

options.A: Active scanning tools that probe the target's network
options.B: Breach data aggregation services that index leaked credentials and personal data from known compromises
options.C: Vulnerability scanners that identify software flaws
options.E: None of the above

questions.explanation: Dehashed and Intelligence X (IntelX) are breach data aggregation platforms that collect and index leaked data from known compromises, paste sites, and other sources. They allow testers to search for exposed credentials and data associated with a target domain or email addresses.

questions.question: A penetration tester is building employee profiles for a social engineering campaign. Which social media platform is most likely to provide detailed information about an employee's job title, department, technical skills, and professional connections?

options.B: LinkedIn
options.E: All of the above

questions.explanation: LinkedIn is the primary professional networking platform and typically contains detailed employment history, job titles, departments, technical skills, certifications, and professional connections — all highly valuable for crafting targeted social engineering attacks.

questions.question: A tester discovers that a target organisation's IT administrator regularly posts photos of their home office on Instagram. One photo clearly shows sticky notes with passwords on the monitor. What OSINT technique has the tester applied?

options.B: Visual intelligence (IMINT) from social media imagery
options.E: Only after formal approval from the board of directors

questions.explanation: Analysing images posted on social media for intelligence is a form of imagery intelligence (IMINT). Photos may inadvertently reveal credentials, internal systems, security badges, building layouts, or hardware details useful for an engagement.

questions.question: Which OSINT framework is commonly used to automate the collection and correlation of social media profiles, email addresses, and online identities associated with a target individual?

options.B: Wireshark
options.E: This is not a requirement for CREST certification

questions.explanation: Maltego is a visual link analysis and OSINT tool that automates the collection of information from social media, DNS, WHOIS, and other sources, presenting relationships between entities in a graph format. It is widely used for mapping individuals' online presence.

questions.question: A penetration tester uses a tool to extract geolocation data from photos posted by target employees on Twitter/X. The GPS coordinates reveal that multiple employees frequent a specific coffee shop near the office. How could this intelligence be used ethically within a sanctioned engagement?

options.A: To physically surveil and follow the employees
options.B: To inform a physical social engineering scenario (e.g., tailgating or rogue Wi-Fi deployment) if physical testing is within the agreed scope
options.C: To report the employees to their employer for security violations
options.D: This information has no practical use in penetration testing
options.E: It depends on the specific country's jurisdiction

questions.explanation: If physical security testing is within scope, geolocation intelligence from social media can inform realistic scenarios such as setting up a rogue access point at the coffee shop or planning a tailgating attempt. All actions must remain within the agreed rules of engagement.

questions.question: During LinkedIn reconnaissance, a tester notices that the target company has recently posted multiple job listings for 'Kubernetes administrator' and 'AWS security engineer'. What can be inferred from this information?

options.A: The company is going bankrupt and laying off staff
options.B: The company likely uses or is migrating to Kubernetes on AWS, and may currently have gaps in their cloud security team
options.C: The company has already been compromised
options.D: The company does not use any cloud services
options.E: Only when using automated scanning tools

questions.explanation: Job listings reveal technology stack information (Kubernetes, AWS), indicate potential gaps in staffing for security roles, and suggest current or planned infrastructure. A gap in security staffing may indicate reduced monitoring or misconfigured security controls.

questions.question: A tester is using theHarvester tool during the reconnaissance phase. Which combination of data sources does theHarvester collect from?

options.A: Only DNS records and WHOIS data
options.B: Search engines, PGP key servers, LinkedIn, and other public sources to gather emails, subdomains, hosts, and employee names
options.E: This is handled by the client's internal IT department

questions.explanation: theHarvester is a versatile OSINT gathering tool that queries search engines (Google, Bing), PGP key servers, LinkedIn, Shodan, and other public sources to collect email addresses, subdomains, hostnames, employee names, and open ports associated with a target domain.

questions.question: A penetration tester uses exiftool to analyse a PDF document downloaded from the target's public website. The metadata reveals 'Author: jsmith', 'Creator: Microsoft Word 2019', and 'Producer: Adobe PDF Library 15.0'. What reconnaissance value does this provide?

options.A: No value; metadata is automatically generated and meaningless
options.B: A potential username (jsmith), the document creation software (Word 2019), and evidence of a Windows environment with Adobe products
options.E: During the post-engagement debrief session

questions.explanation: Document metadata can reveal usernames (which may map to Active Directory accounts), software versions in use (informing OS and application targeting), internal printer names, and file paths — all valuable intelligence for the penetration test.

questions.question: Which tool is specifically designed to extract metadata from documents found on a target's website by first using search engines to discover publicly available files?

options.B: FOCA (Fingerprinting Organizations with Collected Archives)
options.E: Only if the vulnerability is classified as Critical

questions.explanation: FOCA uses search engine dorking to find documents published by a target organisation, downloads them, and extracts metadata including usernames, software versions, email addresses, internal paths, printer names, and operating system details.

questions.question: A tester uses metagoofil to download and analyse documents from a target domain. The tool discovers internal file paths such as 'C:\Users\admin\Documents\ProjectX\' in multiple Word documents. What does this reveal?

options.A: The documents were created on Linux systems
options.B: Internal Windows file system paths, a username ('admin'), and a project name ('ProjectX') that may aid further enumeration
options.C: The web server is running on the C: drive
options.D: The documents are encrypted with BitLocker
options.E: This is a standard feature of most antivirus software

questions.explanation: Embedded file paths in document metadata reveal operating system (Windows), local usernames, directory structures, and project naming conventions. The username 'admin' could be tested against authentication services, and 'ProjectX' may help identify related resources.
